title: Blood Test Detects 90% of Early-Stage Pancreatic Cancers, Japanese Study Finds
excerpt: Researchers at Kanazawa University developed a whole-blood gene expression test that outperformed existing markers in catching the deadliest common cancer at its most treatable stage.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A new blood test detects 90% of early-stage pancreatic cancers, outperforming the CA19-9 marker.
  • Gene expression changes in blood immune cells signal cancer presence even with normal CA19-9 levels.
  • Five-year survival for stage 0 pancreatic cancer is 100%, highlighting the importance of early detection.
  • The commercial test, Panregza, is already available in Japan, developed by Cubix Inc.

  • A whole-blood mRNA test detected 90% of stage 0–I pancreatic cancers, compared to just 10% for the standard CA19-9 marker.
  • Kanazawa University researchers found that gene expression changes in blood immune cells occur even when tumors are tiny and CA19-9 levels are normal.
  • Five-year survival for stage 0 pancreatic cancer is 100% at the study center, compared to 13% overall — making early detection critical.
  • A commercial version of the test, called Panregza, is already being marketed in Japan by Cubix Inc.

Pancreatic cancer kills roughly 87% of those diagnosed with it, largely because there is no reliable way to catch it early. By the time symptoms appear — jaundice, unexplained weight loss, abdominal pain — the cancer has usually spread beyond the organ. A new study from Japan offers what researchers call the strongest evidence yet that a simple blood draw can change that equation.

A Gene Signature in the Blood

Researchers at Kanazawa University Hospital analyzed whole-blood gene expression patterns using a panel of 56 mRNA probes. In a pilot validation study of patients with stage 0 and stage I pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the test correctly identified 9 out of 10 cases — a 90% detection rate.

By comparison, the widely used tumor marker CA19-9 caught just 1 in 10 early-stage cases. The combined test, marketed commercially in Japan as Panregza, showed 60% sensitivity and 93.3% specificity.

"This diagnostic test enables early detection of pancreatic cancer and is not dependent on tumor volume."

— Kanazawa University research team

Why Early Detection Matters So Much

The survival gap in pancreatic cancer is starker than in almost any other malignancy. At Kanazawa University Hospital's Innovative Research and Development Center for Pancreatic Cancer, patients diagnosed at stage 0 have a five-year survival rate of 100%. Those caught at stage I survive at 74.4%. The overall five-year survival rate — when most patients are diagnosed at advanced stages — hovers around 13%.

The pancreas sits deep in the abdomen, produces few early symptoms, and sheds limited biomarkers into the bloodstream. CT scans and endoscopic ultrasound are expensive, invasive, and impractical for routine screening.

How the Science Works

The test relies on a key biological insight: pancreatic tumors alter gene expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, the immune cells circulating in the bloodstream. The Kanazawa team had previously shown that these expression patterns differ between cancer patients and healthy individuals.

This latest study established that these changes occur even at the earliest cancer stages, when tumor burden is minimal and standard biomarkers show nothing abnormal. The immune system signals the cancer's presence before the tumor is large enough to shed detectable proteins.

A Parallel Track in the United States

Separately, researchers at City of Hope in California have developed a complementary approach using exosome-based microRNA markers. In a study of nearly 1,000 participants across four countries, their liquid biopsy detected about 90% of early-stage pancreatic cancers. When combined with CA19-9, accuracy rose to 97%, according to data presented at the American Association for Cancer Research annual meeting.

That test, led by molecular diagnostics specialist Ajay Goel, has been licensed to Pharus Diagnostics for commercial development.

What This Means for High-Risk Populations

Neither test is ready for mass population screening. Experts say the immediate application is for people at elevated risk — those with a family history of pancreatic cancer, certain genetic mutations like BRCA2, chronic pancreatitis, or newly diagnosed diabetes after age 50.

For South Asians, the relevance is direct. Higher rates of type 2 diabetes in the community represent a known risk factor for pancreatic cancer. A blood test administered during a routine checkup, without expensive imaging, could lower the barrier to screening significantly.

Pancreatic cancer remains the third-leading cause of cancer death in the United States. A test that shifts diagnosis from stage IV to stage 0 would represent one of the most consequential advances in oncology in years.
